la:verb:ligo.html:
lĭgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
Gr. root λυγin λύγος, λυγόω
,
to tie, bind, bind together,

bind up, bandage, bind fast, etc. (syn.: vincio, destino; perh. only poet. and post-Aug. prose).

Lit.: manus post terga ligatae,: ligare et vincire crura et manus,: crus fasciā,: laqueo guttura,to tie up,: vulnera veste,to bind up, bandage,: dum mula ligatur,is harnessed,: funem litoribus,: sudarium circum collum,to bind around,: pisces in glacie ligatos,i. e. frozen fast,: nimbi ligati,i. e. ice,.—
Transf., to wind round, to surround: balteus loricam ligat,: digitosque ligat junctura,; .—
To fix or fasten in: igne cremato lapide caementa in tectis ligantur,.—
Trop., to bind up, bind together, unite: dissociata locis concordi pace ligavit,: vinclo propiore cum aliquo ligari,: laqueo colla,.—
To ratify, confirm: pacta,conjugia artibus magicis,: argumenta in catenas, * .—Hence, P. a.: lĭgātus, a, um, connected with, adjoining: Tartari ripis ligatos squalidae mortis specus,.

la:noun:lignum.html:
lignum, i, n.
prob. root leg-, v. 2. lĕgo; that which is gathered, i. e. for firewood
,
wood (firewood. opp. to materia, timber for building, ).
Lit. (class. only in plur.): ligna neque fumosa erunt et ardebunt bene,: ligna et sarmenta circumdare, ignem subicere,: ignem ex lignis viridibus atque umidis fieri jussit,, § 45: ligna super foco Large reponens,: ligna et virgas et carbones quibusdam videri esse in penu, Mas. Sab. ap. .—Prov.: in silvam ligna ferre, i. e. to perform useless labor, or, as we say in English, to carry coals to Newcastle, : lignorum aliquid posce,.—
In gen., timber, wood: hos lignum stabat in usus, Annosam si forte nucem dejecerat Eurus,i. e. for making tables,.—
Transf.
That which is made of wood, a writing-tablet: vana supervacui dicunt chirographa ligni,; ; a plank: ventis animam committe, dolato confisus ligno,.—
The hard part of fruit, the shell (of a nut), or the stone or kernel (of cherries, plums, etc.): bacarum intus lignum,; : lignum in pomo,; of grape-stones, .—
A fault in table-tops, where the grain of the wood is not curly, but straight, .—
(Poet. and late Lat.) A tree, ; ; : lignum pomiferum,: lignum scientiae boni et mali,: lignum vitae,.—
A staff, club (eccl. Lat.): cum gladiis et lignis, and 48.

† Lĭgerĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Liger, Ligerian, Inscr. ap. Grut. 472, 1.

la:verb:ligurio.html:
lĭgūrĭo and lĭgurrĭo, īvi and ĭi, ītum (
impers. ligurribant, ), 4, v. a. and n.
root lig-; cf. lingo
, to lick. *
Neutr., to be dainty, fond of good things (cf. lambo): quae (meretrices) cum amatore cum cenant, liguriunt,.—
Act., to lick.
Lit.: apes non, ut muscae, (eum) liguriunt,: semesos pisces tepidumque jus,.—
Transf.: dum ruri rurant homines, quos (parasiti) liguriant,whom they lick, whom they daintily feed upon,: furta,to lick up, feast on by stealth,.—Also in mal. part., as Gr. λείχειν and λειχάζειν, ; .—
Trop., to long for, desire eagerly, lust after any thing: improbissima lucra liguriens,: agrariam curationem,.
